hello.note: Literally close to 'are you well'; also heard as the Swahili loan Jambo/Mambo in Mwanza town.

good_morning.note: The ng' is one nasal sound, as in 'sing'. A Sukuma-English wordlist spells this Ng'wangaloka (u/o vowel variant); same word, unstandardized orthography.

good_evening.note: Same word covers 'good afternoon'; context marks the difference.

goodbye.note: Literally 'we'll see each other'; a Sukuma-English wordlist independently gives Tukwibona (same word, plain-b spelling) as the standing translation of 'see you', so the standalone form is now corroborated, not just reconstructed from Tukwibhona badae (see you later) / Tukwibhona ntondo (see you tomorrow).

how_are_you.note: The bh/mh sounds are soft, breathy b/m. Mwadila mhola? is the evening version.

youre_welcome.note: A Sukuma-English wordlist gives Tuliho as an interjection meaning 'welcome', the best-attested candidate; it likely also covers the reply-to-thanks role the way Swahili karibu does in the same region, but that exact function is not separately confirmed. Makaribu, a Sukuma-shaped take on Swahili karibu, is heard too but is an unattested blend rather than a sourced form, so it was dropped as the lead pick.

no_problem.note: Literally 'there's no trouble': nduhu is the negation-existential ('there isn't') and tabhu is the Swahili loan taabu (trouble; compare hakuna tabu, 'there is no problem', in Swahili). Both pieces check out individually but the compound itself is a plausible calque, not an independently attested fixed phrase, so treat with some caution.

please.note: Closer to 'I'm asking/begging you'; Sukuma leans on requesting verbs rather than a bare 'please', as in Nalilomba ghinu (I need a favour, please).

excuse_me.note: The Swahili word itself, used as-is; no separate Sukuma form turned up in sources.

sorry.note: Same word covers both 'excuse me' and 'sorry', just like in Swahili.

yes.note: No distinct native Sukuma word for a bare 'yes' surfaced in available sources; this is the shared regional affirmation also used in Swahili. Treat with caution.

no.note: A native Kisukuma teaching video gives Biya and Yaya as ways to say 'no'; sourcing is thin, so treat as a lead rather than settled fact.

of_course.note: The Swahili phrase, used as-is; no distinct Sukuma equivalent was found in sources.

amazing.note: The root -wiza (good) recurs across sourced phrases (Ng'waka gwawiza, Ubhize na lushiku lwa wiza); here reconstructed as a standalone exclamation, so confidence is moderate.

delicious.note: The Swahili phrase; sources only show food praised indirectly, e.g. Ilikhubhi ili liza (this vegetable is good), with no dedicated Sukuma 'delicious' word found.

cheers.note: The Swahili toast, used across Tanzania including Sukumaland; no distinct Sukuma form found in sources.
